translations: School life was highly regimented. The wake-up bell rang at 6 a.m., and twenty minutes later we assembled on the playground for morning exercises, followed by breakfast. Classes ran from 8 to noon. After a thirty-minute rest following lunch, classes resumed until 4:30 p.m., when students were free. Most headed to the playground for basketball or stayed in the classroom to study; some simply talked with classmates. Dinner was at 6 p.m., and from 7 to 9 we were required to read in the classroom. Lights out came at 9:30. Before exams, some students would secretly light candles in their dorms and pull all-nighters, which was against the rules. From Sunday evening through Saturday noon each week, students had to remain on campus unless specially excused. A few bolder souls, myself included, sometimes slipped over the school fence after lights out to grab a late-night snack from a shop outside, but once a disciplinary officer on patrol caught me, I received a minor demerit that was posted on the bulletin board. I found it deeply humiliating and never tried to sneak out again.

To my surprise, I had done remarkably well in the summer session. When the program ended, the school recommended me for formal admission as a second-year student, and a great weight lifted off my shoulders. My parents were overjoyed, and my mother especially felt she had earned considerable face among her friends.

I spent two and a half years at Nankai, from the first year of junior high through the first year of senior high—from the summer of 1943 to the winter of 1945, spanning the still-harsh years of the war to the period after victory. It was my first time living away from home, my first taste of relative independence, and my first experience of communal life from morning till night. It was also the first time I stepped out from my parents' shelter. Life was austere, but my spirits soared. We called ourselves the future masters of China in an age of great transformation. By then the final outcome seemed never in doubt, and China's standing in the world had risen rapidly since Pearl Harbor to join the ranks of the "Four Great Powers." Shortly after I enrolled, Chairman Chiang Kai-shek attended the Cairo Conference, sitting alongside President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill as an equal. The news electrified the country. After more than a century of humiliation at the hands of the Western powers, China was finally rising. We young people felt the weight of nation-building resting squarely on our shoulders.

The teachers at Nankai were distinguished in both scholarship and spirit, and all commanded the deep respect of their students. Two left particularly vivid impressions on me. Our Chinese literature teacher was a quite young woman from Tongcheng in Anhui province. She made the prose of the Tongcheng School—which was notorious for its obscurity and difficulty—come alive with genuine zest and charm. The other was our music teacher. At that time Disney's Fantasia had just been released and was playing in the movie theaters in Chongqing. The film used animated cartoons to introduce classical masterworks, awakening a passion for classical music in audiences who had never had any contact with it. Our teacher went to see the film and returned to school buzzing with enthusiasm, passionately recommending it to us. I can still see her radiant, animated expression as she described it.
